says: Five independent readers of the recorded sessions exist where one shared reader is imported by nineteen packages, and three of the four extras have a real reason: one needs per step token fields the shared record does not carry, one needs occupancy and fork and compaction and reads through the session store instead, and one is a byte scan for a quota key rather than a turn parse. Only one re-walks by hand what the shared walker already does, and that is a clean merge. The most repeated shape is the smallest: six separate declarations of a skip record holding a path and a reason, with two pairs sharing a name across different packages. Two apparent duplications are left alone with arguments: a nearest rank percentile over integers is correct where an interpolated float one is not, because a fractional value between two byte counts means nothing. One thing that looks like duplication is named as not being any: four packages sum a cost with the same loop, and each sums a different field on a different struct answering a different question, so a shared helper would save one line per site and put a layer between the reader and the field. Nothing was merged, deleted or rewritten: the deliverable is the list and the judgment.

says: The ledger holds 2,780 decision rows and 20 of them carry an outcome, all hand labelled and all attached to tool_gate. Exactly one labelled row sits near a threshold, within three dead bands of risk_deny_at, and none sits near risk_ask_at; stop_check and shell_sift have none at all. A threshold needs roughly 60 labels near its operating point at a 5 percent false positive budget and 300 at 1 percent, so no point is calibratable at either and tool_gate alone needs 59 more near one threshold and 60 near the other. The reach of three dead bands is argued rather than assumed: one dead band is the tie zone the decision code already uses, so a label sitting inside it proves nothing about where the line should sit. There is no arrival rate, because all 20 outcomes were written in a 78 second window five days ago and nothing since, with nineteen of them inside two seconds, which the report calls consistent with a scripted loop rather than a person. Its conclusion is that hand labelling cannot close the gap and the shadow gate writing outcomes automatically is the path that scales. It also found that the ask point has never written a ledger row at all, which is a missing writer rather than a labelling gap.

says: No recorded session has ever come near the context ceiling: the highest peak is 66,162 tokens, 26.5 percent of the 250,000 limit, and the median is 20,179, 8.1 percent. Zero sessions reached half the ceiling, one reached a quarter and fifteen reached a tenth. Two sessions did cross the compaction target in force when they ran, 66,162 against 63,000 and 57,326 against 50,000, and the two targets differ because the band shares in konst moved between them. Nothing has ever been evicted by the in-place rewrite: zero compaction events on any step of any recorded session. What ran twice instead was the fork, which isolates and continues, matching the two crossings one for one. The re-fetch rate is therefore defined rather than undefined, and it is 0 of 2: neither continuation repeated a pre-fork tool call, and the one time one wanted old material it fetched the artifact handle the carry already held. The condition under which this starts to matter is named: a session several times longer than any recorded, a smaller ceiling, a model with a smaller window, or a task reading much larger results than this corpus of many small calls.

says: The tool schemas a turn sends cost 16,575 bytes on every request, about 4,143 tokens for all 18 tools, and deferring them is not worth building. The figure is measured by encoding a real request with and without the tools array and taking the difference; summing the tools individually gives 16,492, and the 83 byte gap is the array's own brackets and commas. Caching is what decides it: on the measured turn the block was written to cache once on step one and never again across eleven steps, and 81.6 percent of that turn's billed input was cache reads. Across the corpus, 24 recorded turns wrote to cache and 23 of them made a second model call and read the write back; at today's 18 tool scale, 14 of 15 did. The deferral mechanism is named and costed rather than assumed: a catalog line plus a fetch before first use would have added 5 round trips to the measured turn to save at most 2,873 tokens, paid once at cache-write price. The only case it would pay is a turn that makes exactly one model call and never returns, which was 1 of 24.

says: Jev scored 25 of 27 against a regular expression's 24 of 27 on a corpus of real recorded tool results, and a rerun minutes later tied both arms at 24, so the report's conclusion is that the corpus cannot decide this rather than that the judgment won. Both arms score high because this project's recorded sessions carry almost no adversarial instruction-shaped text: what looks like a directive is nearly always the harness's own scaffolding, an oversized-result notice, a bash-timeout caution or a refused-citation notice, never a planted attack. Neither arm's mistakes sit inside the other's: the regular expression's three misses are directive-shaped words inside ordinary Go source or a test assertion rather than text addressed to a reader, and jev's two misses are the same refused-citation caution scored at 0.18, under its own line, which the literal word match caught. The two-task test found no separation, 0.03 to 0.06 apart on three cases, which is the opposite of what the shell sift found. Deciding two arms that both score in the high eighties needs a few hundred labelled cases, and this corpus is 27. It cost $0.000935 over 27 live calls.

says: Running four candidate search patterns over the whole tree costs 320 ms against 14 ms for the literal, so the plan's claim that they cost nothing is false as written and the first implementation spent 638 ms of candidate scan on an 819 ms call. Each form now runs only where it can change the answer: the word boundary and go symbol forms match a subset of the literal, so they are free at 11 ms of a 165 ms call against 131 ms spent reading files. Over 20 replayed recorded searches, 6 returned nothing and a candidate form rescued 0 of them: not one was a case error. says: 67 of 1412 recorded tool calls failed, 4.7%, and 74.6% of those failures carry no reason beyond a bare nonzero exit code. Every failure that carries any error text at all classifies cleanly into bad arguments, not found in this environment or timeout; the whole unknown share is bash calls that exited nonzero with an empty Error field, a number the harness already has and never types. edit is the worst tool among those with at least 5 calls, 11 of 55, 20.0%, every one of them an anchor or an occurrence count that no longer matches the file. The categories cannot express the admin-template shape named in the ticket, a run of calls that succeed as a process and fail as work: this project's own corpus holds the same pattern in turn-18d6ea32da3230c0 and turn-18d6e1de4b235b54, hunting for a go binary, and only the probes that happened to exit nonzero land in this report at all.

says: There is nothing to save because there is nothing there: tofu's read tool never prefixes a line with its number. A whole read returns the file bytes verbatim and a ranged read prepends one header line. Over 296 read calls in 110 recorded turns, line-number bytes are 0, which is 0.0 percent of 1,016,862 read-tool bytes and 0.0 percent of 9,257,594 cache-read tokens. The threshold was stated first, under 0.5 percent is a no. The pasted claim of 1.6 percent described a harness that numbers every line, which two clones do behind a flag that is off by default, and neither they nor any other clone numbers sparsely.

says: Against a 100 ms threshold chosen before measuring, every shape crosses it: shell resolution median 101.5 ms and worst 135.3 ms over 12 samples, the go toolchain probe median 172.9 ms and worst 201.2 ms, the node toolchain probe with node and npm median 780.7 ms and worst 904.7 ms, both over 6 rounds. So a node project waits about eight tenths of a second before the first token, paid once per session, for a line in the environment block. The figures are derived rather than directly timed: NewBashTool is timed on an empty directory and on the project directory back to back, because resolveShell and probeToolchain have no exported seam, and the probe figure is the delta.

says: Naming the reason at the moment a command exits moves the unclassifiable share of tool failures from 74.6 percent to 71.6, 50 failures to 48, over the same 1,412 calls and 67 failures. The recovery is small on purpose: only 2 of the 50 bare failures carried exit 127 or 126, and the other 48 are exit 1 or 2, which mean nothing on their own and stay unknown. The gain is on calls made from now on, where the harness records not found in this environment or found but not executable rather than a number, and the same fallback reads records already on disk so the corpus improves without a rewrite.

says: Starting the toolchain probe in the background moves the wait rather than removing it, and the report says so. Constructing the bash tool on a node project is now a median of 0.5 ms and a worst of 6.0, against 780.7 and 904.7 before. Realized, meaning construction plus the first read of the answer in a fresh directory, it is a median of 722.0 ms and a worst of 768.5: the same work, paid when the answer is first needed. What is genuinely saved is a second turn in the same directory sharing one cache, a median of 89.0 ms and a worst of 95.0. Shell resolution is a median of 96.0 ms. A person feels none of this yet, because cmd/tofu/run.go still resolves and probes twice per session and shares no cache.
